proof of attendance.definition: A token issued as a record that someone was present at an event, popularized by the POAP standard. It is a collectible marker rather than a financial asset.

proof-of-work (pow).definition: A security mechanism for blockchains that requires nodes to expend energy in the form of computation to find a certain value.

protocol.definition: The set of rules Ethereum clients implement so that independent nodes agree on the same state. It covers block structure, transaction validity, the EVM, consensus, and networking, and changes only through coordinated upgrades.
protocol.translation_note: The set of rules governing the Ethereum network. NOT a medical or diplomatic protocol.

prysm.definition: A Go consensus client for Ethereum, and one of the earliest implementations of the Beacon Chain. It is a product name.
prysm.note: Go-based consensus client. Product name, do not translate meaning.

public goods.definition: Public goods are things everyone can use for free, like parks or clean air, and using them doesn’t stop others from using them too. Governments often provide these because businesses usually won’t, since they can’t easily charge people for using them.

re-entrancy attack.definition: An attack that consists of an attacker contract calling a victim contract function in such a way that during execution the victim calls the attacker contract again, recursively. This can result, for example, in the theft of funds by skipping parts of the victim contract that update balances or count withdrawal amounts.

real world assets (rwa).definition: Offchain assets such as treasury bills, real estate, or invoices represented as tokens on a blockchain. Because the asset itself lives offchain, the arrangement rests on a legal claim and an issuer.

recursive length prefix (rlp).definition: An encoding standard designed by the Ethereum developers to encode and serialize objects (data structures) of arbitrary complexity and length.

regenerative finance (refi).definition: Applying onchain finance to fund ecological and social restoration, for example by tokenizing carbon credits or directing protocol revenue toward public goods. The aim is to make regeneration economically self-sustaining.

reth.definition: A Rust execution client for Ethereum, built as a modular library as well as a runnable node. It is a product name.
reth.note: Rust-based execution client. Product name, do not translate meaning.

retroactive public goods funding (rpgf).definition: Rewarding work after it has demonstrably produced value, rather than funding proposals in advance. Judging impact in hindsight is easier than predicting it, so the model is used to fund open-source and ecosystem contributions.

reward.definition: An amount of ether awarded to validators that perform certain functions, including proposing a block or participating in a sync-committee, in each slot.

self-sovereignty.definition: Holding and controlling your own identity, keys, and assets directly, without depending on an institution to hold them for you. It carries both the authority and the responsibility for their security.

sepolia.definition: An Ethereum test network used for application and contract testing, run by a permissioned validator set. Its ETH has no value and is obtained from faucets.
sepolia.note: Ethereum testnet. Network name, keep Latin.

serialization.definition: The process of converting a data structure into a sequence of bytes.

snark.definition: Short for "succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge", a SNARK is a type of zero-knowledge proof.

soft fork.definition: A divergence in a blockchain that occurs when the consensus rules change. Contrary to a hard fork, a soft fork is backwards compatible; upgraded nodes can validate blocks created by non-upgraded nodes as long as they follow the new consensus rules.
soft fork.morph_note: Often loanword as noun but translated as 'divergence' as verb in RU/PL

stark.definition: Short for "scalable transparent argument of knowledge", a STARK is a type of zero-knowledge proof.

state bloat.definition: Growth of the Ethereum state database making it harder for nodes to store and process
state bloat.translation_note: 'Bloat' translated as 'swelling' or 'illness' in many languages

state-expiry.definition: Proposals to make state that has not been touched for a long time inactive, so nodes no longer have to keep all of it on hand. Reviving expired state would require supplying a proof of its prior contents.
state-expiry.note: Mechanism to remove old state data from nodes to reduce storage requirements.

statelessness.definition: A design goal where nodes don't need to store the full state to validate blocks
statelessness.translation_note: Must not imply 'no status' or 'no country'

swarm.definition: A decentralized storage and communication network for Ethereum applications, used to host content and data offchain while referencing it onchain.

sybil attack.definition: Sybil attacks refer to individual humans tricking a system into thinking they are multiple people to increase their influence.

syncing.definition: The process of downloading the entire latest version of a blockchain to a node.
syncing.morph_note: Long formal word for noun vs short English-derived slang for verb/action

szabo.definition: A denomination of ether. 1 szabo = 10<sup>12</sup> wei. 10<sup>6</sup> szabo = 1 ether.
szabo.note: Denomination of ether (lowercase). Named after Nick Szabo (proper noun when referring to the person).

teku.definition: A Java consensus client for Ethereum, aimed at institutional and staking operators. It is a product name.
teku.note: Java-based consensus client. Product name, do not translate meaning.

terminal total difficulty (ttd).definition: The total difficulty is the sum of the Ethash mining difficulty for all blocks up to some specific point in the blockchain. The terminal total difficulty is a specific value for the total difficulty that was used as the trigger for execution clients to switch off their mining and block gossip functions enabling the network to transition to proof-of-stake. It is no longer relevant because Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake.

testnet.definition: Short for "test network," a network used to simulate the behavior of the main Ethereum network.
testnet.translation_note: A test network for development. Opposite of mainnet.

total value locked (tvl).definition: The aggregate value of assets deposited in a protocol, or across a set of protocols, at a point in time. It is a rough measure of usage, and it moves with token prices as well as with deposits.

trust assumptions.definition: Trust assumptions are basic beliefs about a system's safety and dependability, guiding what we trust for the system to function.

trust-minimized.definition: Describes a system built so that as few parties as possible must be trusted, with the remaining assumptions made explicit and verifiable. It is more accurate than trustless, since some assumptions always remain.
trust-minimized.translation_note: More precise than 'trustless'; 'low trust' sounds like a negative attribute

trustless.definition: Describes an interaction whose correctness you can verify yourself instead of having to trust a counterparty. The term is common but imprecise; trust-minimized is usually the better word.

turing complete.definition: A concept named after English mathematician and computer scientist Alan Turing - a system of data-manipulation rules (such as a computer's instruction set, a programming language, or a cellular automaton) is said to be "Turing complete" or "computationally universal" if it can be used to simulate any Turing machine.
turing complete.note: Turing is always capitalized (proper noun from Alan Turing).

utxo.definition: The unspent transaction output model, used by Bitcoin, in which the ledger is a set of discrete spendable outputs rather than account balances. Ethereum instead uses an account model, tracking a balance and nonce per account.

web 3.0.definition: An older label for web3, the model of web applications built on public blockchains where users hold their own keys, assets, and identity. Prefer web3 in new writing.
web 3.0.note: Alias for Web3. Prefer "web3" (standard casing) for new content. "Web 3.0" is acceptable but not preferred.

web2.definition: Is the current internet, focused on user-generated content and social media that are controlled by few companies. Web3 is a crypto belief that users should control their data and transactions instead.

whitepaper.definition: A document setting out the design and rationale of a protocol or project. The Ethereum Whitepaper, written by Vitalik Buterin in 2013, describes the idea of a blockchain with a general-purpose programmable state.
whitepaper.note: "Ethereum Whitepaper" is a proper noun (published work). A general "whitepaper" is standard casing.

witness.definition: The data needed to verify a state access without holding the full state: the values read plus the proofs that they belong to the state root. Stateless client designs depend on witnesses being small enough to ship alongside a block.
witness.note: In Verkle tree context: proof data needed to verify a state access without full state.

yellow paper.definition: The formal specification of Ethereum, written by Gavin Wood, defining the EVM and the state transition function in mathematical notation. It is the precise counterpart to the more informal whitepaper.
yellow paper.note: "Ethereum Yellow Paper" is a proper noun (published work). A general "yellow paper" is standard casing.

decentralized autonomous organization (d.definition:
A DAO is a digital organization run by rules coded on a blockchain, where decisions are made by member votes, not a central authority.
Each member's voting power often tied to the number of tokens they hold. DAOs aim to democratize decision-making and operations, focusing on transparency and community governance.
decentralized autonomous organization (d.translation_note: Organization governed by smart contract rules and member votes. 'DAO' stays Latin.

delegate.definition: Someone entrusted with others' voting power so they can vote on their behalf, and, as a verb, the act of assigning that power. Delegation leaves the underlying tokens with the holder, who can reassign or reclaim the votes at any time.

delegation.definition: Assigning your voting power, or in staking your validation duties, to another party while keeping ownership of the underlying assets. It lets holders take part without acting on every decision themselves.

ethereum improvement proposal (eip).definition: A design document providing information to the Ethereum community, describing a proposed new feature or its processes or environment (see ERC).
ethereum improvement proposal (eip).note: All EIP-n identifiers (EIP-1559, EIP-4844, EIP-7702, etc.) ALWAYS stay in Latin script. Never translate or transliterate the numbered identifier. The expanded form (Ethereum Improvement Proposal) can be translated for explanation. The /api/v1/filter endpoint enforces this programmatically via STANDARD_PATTERNS in src/lib/content-filter.ts: do not add per-instance master entries for specific EIP-N standards (DRY).
ethereum improvement proposal (eip).translation_note: EIP-n identifiers always Latin. Expanded form translatable. Pattern applies to ALL numbered EIPs. Filter matches the family at request time; no per-instance entries needed.

governance.definition: The process by which a protocol or organization decides on changes to its rules, parameters, and funds. Ethereum's own protocol governance runs through open proposals and rough consensus among clients and the community, not onchain voting.

proposal.definition: A formal suggestion put forward for a decision, whether an improvement proposal for the protocol or a motion put to a DAO's voters. It states what should change and, in onchain governance, often the exact calls to execute.
proposal.morph_note: 'Block proposer' translates differently than general 'to propose an idea'

public good.definition: Something anyone can use without reducing its availability to others, such as open-source software or protocol research. Because users cannot readily be charged, public goods are chronically underfunded and depend on grants and similar mechanisms.

quadratic funding.definition: A matching mechanism that allocates a shared pool according to the square of the summed square roots of individual contributions, so the number of distinct contributors counts for more than the size of any single donation. It directs matching funds toward what a community broadly wants.

quadratic voting.definition: Is a voting method where voters express how strongly they feel about issues. It allows voters to show not just preference, but also the intensity of their preference.

randao.definition: The scheme that produces the consensus layer's randomness. Each proposer reveals a signature that is mixed into an accumulating value, so no single participant can determine the result, though the last to reveal can choose to withhold.

treasury.definition: A pool of funds controlled by a protocol or DAO, usually held in a contract and spent only through governance decisions. It funds development, grants, and incentives.

vote.definition: An expression of preference on a proposal, weighted in most DAOs by tokens held or delegated. Votes may be cast onchain, where the result can execute automatically, or offchain as a signal.
vote.morph_note: Governance: 'ballot'(n) vs 'act of voting'(v) use different stems in Finno-Ugric

decentralized identity (did).definition: An approach in which identifiers and credentials are controlled by their subject rather than issued and held by a central provider. It rests on keys the user holds and on credentials that can be verified without contacting the issuer.

ethereum name service (ens).definition:
Ethereum Name Service is like an internet phonebook for Ethereum addresses. Instead of using long wallet addresses, ENS lets you use simple names like "john.eth" to send and receive digital money and assets.

Technical:
The ENS registry is a single central contract that provides a mapping from domain names to owners and resolvers, as described in EIP-137.

kyc.definition: Know your customer: the identity checks that regulated financial services must perform on their users. It applies to intermediaries such as exchanges, not to the Ethereum protocol itself.

siwe.definition: Sign-In with Ethereum, standardized as ERC-4361. It defines a structured message a user signs with their wallet so an application can authenticate them by their address, with no password or identity provider.

stealth-address.definition: A scheme in which a sender derives a fresh, one-time address that only the recipient can spend from, so repeated payments to the same person cannot be linked onchain. ERC-5564 defines how such addresses are generated and announced.
stealth-address.note: Privacy technique generating one-time addresses for each transaction.

verifiable credential.definition: A tamper-evident, cryptographically signed claim about a subject that can be checked against the issuer's key. The holder decides when to present it, and selective disclosure can reveal only part of what it asserts.

back-running.definition: Placing a transaction immediately after a known pending transaction to profit from the state it creates, such as arbitraging a price a large trade has just moved. Unlike front-running, it does not delay or worsen the original transaction.

front-running.definition: Observing a pending transaction and getting your own executed first in order to profit from it. A public mempool makes this possible, because pending transactions are visible before they are included.

maximal extractable value (mev).definition: The maximum value that can be extracted from block production in excess of the standard block reward and gas fees by including, excluding, and changing the order of transactions in a block.
maximal extractable value (mev).translation_note: Value extracted by reordering/inserting transactions in a block. 'MEV' stays Latin.

mev-boost.definition: Middleware that lets a validator outsource block building: it collects bids from builders through relays and signs the header of the highest bid without seeing the block's contents. It is how proposer-builder separation is done today, ahead of any in-protocol version.
mev-boost.note: Software for proposer-builder separation. Product name, do not translate.

sandwich attack.definition: Placing one transaction before a victim's trade and another immediately after it, moving the price against the victim and capturing the difference. Tight slippage limits and private transaction routing are the usual defenses.

searcher.definition: A participant who scans pending transactions and chain state for profitable opportunities, then submits bundles of transactions to builders and pays for their inclusion. Searchers compete on both speed and the size of their bids.

berlin.definition: An Ethereum upgrade activated in April 2021. It repriced several opcodes to better reflect their real cost and introduced typed transaction envelopes together with access lists.

byzantium.definition: The first part of the Metropolis upgrade, activated in October 2017. It added cryptographic precompiles enabling zero-knowledge proofs, the REVERT opcode, and a status field in transaction receipts, and under EIP-649 it delayed the difficulty bomb by a year while reducing the block reward from 5 to 3 ETH.

cancun.definition: The execution-layer half of the Dencun upgrade, activated in March 2024. It introduced blob-carrying transactions under EIP-4844, along with transient storage and other opcode changes.

constantinople.definition: The second part of the Metropolis upgrade, activated in February 2019. It reduced the block reward, added bitwise shifting opcodes and CREATE2, and delayed the difficulty bomb.

ethereum request for comments (erc).definition:
ERC (Ethereum Request for Comments) is a type of technical documentation used in the Ethereum community to propose new standards of usage for the Ethereum network.

These proposals can cover a wide range of topics, including new token standards (like ERC-20 used for tokens and ERC-721 for NFTs).
ethereum request for comments (erc).note: All ERC-n identifiers (ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-1155, etc.) ALWAYS stay in Latin script. Never translate or transliterate the numbered identifier. The expanded form (Ethereum Request for Comments) can be translated for explanation. The /api/v1/filter endpoint enforces this programmatically via STANDARD_PATTERNS in src/lib/content-filter.ts: do not add per-instance master entries for specific ERC-N standards (DRY).
ethereum request for comments (erc).translation_note: ERC-n identifiers always Latin. Expanded form translatable. Pattern applies to ALL numbered ERCs. Filter matches the family at request time; no per-instance entries needed.

fusaka.definition: An Ethereum upgrade combining Fulu on the consensus layer with Osaka on the execution layer. Its headline change is PeerDAS, which lets nodes sample blob data instead of downloading all of it.
fusaka.note: Planned Ethereum upgrade combining Fulu and Osaka. Portmanteau name.

glamsterdam.definition: A planned Ethereum upgrade, named as a portmanteau of its consensus-layer and execution-layer components. Its contents are still being settled through the specification process.

homestead.definition: The second development stage of Ethereum, launched in March 2016 at block 1,150,000.

istanbul.definition: An Ethereum upgrade activated in December 2019. It repriced several opcodes against denial-of-service concerns and made the precompiles used for zero-knowledge cryptography cheaper.

pectra.definition: The upgrade combining Prague on the execution layer with Electra on the consensus layer. It brought account-abstraction features to externally owned accounts under EIP-7702 and raised the maximum effective balance for validators under EIP-7251.
pectra.note: Ethereum upgrade combining Prague (execution) and Electra (consensus). Portmanteau name.

shanghai.definition: The execution-layer half of the Shapella upgrade, activated in April 2023. It enabled staked ETH to be withdrawn from the consensus layer.

shapella.definition: The upgrade activated in April 2023, combining Shanghai on the execution layer with Capella on the consensus layer. It made staking withdrawals possible, completing the transition begun at The Merge.
shapella.note: Ethereum upgrade combining Shanghai (execution) and Capella (consensus). Enabled staking withdrawals.

the merge.definition: The September 2022 upgrade that replaced Ethereum's proof-of-work consensus with proof-of-stake by joining the existing execution chain to the Beacon Chain. It cut the network's energy use by more than 99 percent and changed no account balances or contracts.
the merge.translation_note: The 2022 upgrade transitioning Ethereum from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake. Named event.

verkle trees.definition: A commitment structure proposed to replace Ethereum's Merkle Patricia tries. Vector commitments make proofs far smaller, which is what would make stateless clients practical.

batching.definition: Grouping multiple L2 transactions together for submission to L1
batching.translation_note: 'Stacking' or 'grouping' miss the technical efficiency aspect

blob.definition: A large chunk of data attached to a transaction and made available for a limited period without being readable by the EVM, introduced by EIP-4844. Rollups post their data as blobs because it is far cheaper than calldata and need not be stored forever.
blob.translation_note: Binary large object. In Ethereum: data attached to transactions for L2 scaling (EIP-4844).

blobspace.definition: The blob capacity available in each block, and the market for it. Blobspace is priced by its own fee market, separate from gas, so demand for rollup data does not directly bid up the cost of ordinary transactions.

bridge.definition: A blockchain bridge is used to transfer assets from one blockchain network to another. For example you can use bridge to transfer ETH from the main Ethereum network to cheaper layer 2 scaling solutions.
bridge.morph_note: Physical bridge noun vs functional/computing verb; HU/FI agglutinative suffixes change
bridge.translation_note: Infrastructure for transferring assets between blockchains (noun). Also used as verb ('to bridge tokens'). NOT a physical bridge.

cross-chain.definition: Describes activity spanning two or more separate networks, such as moving assets or passing messages between them. Because each chain verifies only its own state, cross-chain systems must add a mechanism, and a trust assumption, to link them.

dac.definition: A data availability committee: a named group that attests that a chain's transaction data has been published and can be retrieved. It is cheaper than posting data onchain, but users must trust the committee not to withhold it.
dac.note: Data availability committee. Not to be confused with "decentralized autonomous corporation" (rare usage). DAO is the more common term for that concept.

danksharding.definition: The long-term design for scaling Ethereum's data availability, in which a single proposer commits to a large amount of blob data that nodes verify by sampling rather than downloading. EIP-4844 shipped the transaction format and fee market as a first step toward it.

data availability.definition: The guarantee that transaction data has been published in a way that anyone can verify and download. It is critical for rollup security: if the data is unavailable, no one can prove that state transitions are valid.
data availability.translation_note: The guarantee that block data is accessible for verification.

data availability layer.definition: The part of a system responsible for guaranteeing that transaction data has been published where anyone can retrieve it. Without that guarantee, users cannot reconstruct a rollup's state or challenge an invalid one. Ethereum layer 1 is the data availability layer for Ethereum rollups today; some rollups post their data to an alternative layer instead.

data-availability-sampling.definition: A technique in which each node downloads a few random pieces of a large block of data and, from the success of those samples, gains high confidence that all of it is available. Combined with erasure coding, it lets a network verify far more data than any single node stores.
data-availability-sampling.note: Technique allowing nodes to verify data availability without downloading entire blobs.

erasure-coding.definition: Expanding data with redundancy so the original can be reconstructed from any sufficiently large subset of the pieces. It is what makes data availability sampling work: withholding becomes detectable, because an attacker would have to hide a large fraction of the pieces.
erasure-coding.note: Data redundancy technique used in data availability sampling.

escape hatch.definition: Mechanism allowing users to withdraw from an L2 if the sequencer fails
escape hatch.translation_note: Literal translations sound like a physical emergency exit

fault proof.definition: Modern term for fraud proof used by optimistic rollups
fault proof.translation_note: Needs standardization alongside existing 'fraud proof' entry

forced withdrawal.definition: An L2-to-L1 withdrawal that bypasses the sequencer
forced withdrawal.translation_note: Must sound like a 'protocol right' not an 'aggressive act'

interoperability.definition: The ability of separate networks and applications to exchange assets and messages and to work together without a bespoke integration for each pair. It is a central concern for the many rollups settling to Ethereum.

layer 2 (l2).definition: Layer 2s are another networks built on top of Ethereum main network to make transactions faster and cheaper.
layer 2 (l2).translation_note: Networks built on top of Ethereum for scaling. Lowercase, not title-cased.

optimistic rollup.definition: Optimistic Rollup is a layer 2 solution that speeds up transactions on Ethereum, assuming they're valid by default unless challenged.
optimistic rollup.translation_note: L2 scaling solution assuming transactions are valid unless challenged.

peerdas.definition: Peer data availability sampling: a design in which nodes fetch and custody only a subset of each block's blob data from their peers and sample the rest to confirm it is available. It raises the blob capacity a node can support without requiring it to download everything.
peerdas.note: Peer Data Availability Sampling. Protocol name, do not translate.

plasma.definition: An offchain scaling solution that uses fraud proofs, like optimistic rollups. Plasma is limited to simple transactions like basic token transfers and swaps.

proto-danksharding.definition: A new transaction type which accepts "blobs" of data for Ethereum. This "blob" data is temporarily stored on the beacon chain for 4096 epochs (~18.2 days), and can optionally be pruned after to help reduce hardware requirements for node operators.

prover.definition: The party that generates a cryptographic proof that a computation was carried out correctly. Proving is expensive, which is why validity rollups run specialized provers offchain and post only the resulting proof.

rollup.definition: A layer 2 network that executes transactions offchain and posts the data, plus a validity proof or a fraud-proof window, to Ethereum. Users get lower fees while security still derives from Ethereum, because anyone can reconstruct and check the rollup's state from the posted data.
rollup.translation_note: Layer 2 scaling technology that bundles transactions. Always a noun, never used as a verb in Ethereum.

rollups.definition: A type of layer 2 scaling solution that batches multiple transactions and submits them to the Ethereum main chain in a single transaction. This allows for reductions in gas costs and increases in transaction throughput. There are Optimistic and Zero-knowledge rollups which use different security methods to offer these scalability gains.

sequencer.definition: A sequencer is a program responsible for ordering transactions in a blockchain network, particularly within layer 2 scaling solutions.

settlement.definition: The process by which L2 transactions achieve finality on L1
settlement.translation_note: 'Payment' or 'agreement' miss the finality meaning; L2-specific context

sidechain.definition: A scaling solution that uses a separate chain with different, often faster, consensus rules. A bridge is needed to connect these sidechains to Mainnet. Rollups also use sidechains, but they operate in collaboration with Mainnet instead.
sidechain.morph_note: Prefixes 'on-'/'off-' become complex prepositional phrases in TR/HU

state channel.definition: A layer 2 technique in which participants lock funds onchain and then exchange signed state updates directly among themselves, settling onchain only to open and close. It gives instant, feeless interaction, but only within a fixed set of participants who must stay available.

state channels.definition: A layer 2 solution where a channel is set up between participants, where they can transact freely and cheaply. Only a transaction to set up the channel and close the channel is sent to Mainnet. This allows for very high transaction throughput, but does rely on knowing number of participants up front and locking up of funds.

throughput.definition: The number of transactions a network can process per unit of time
throughput.translation_note: 'Performance' or 'yield' too broad; must convey transactions-per-second specifically

validity proof.definition: A security model for certain layer 2 solutions where, to increase speed, transactions are rolled up into batches and submitted to Ethereum in a single transaction. The transaction computation is done offchain and then supplied to the main chain with a proof of their validity. This method increases the amount of transactions possible while maintaining security. Some rollups use fraud proof.

validium.definition: An offchain solution that uses validity proofs to improve transaction throughput. Unlike Zero-knowledge rollups, validium data isn't stored on layer 1 Mainnet.

verifier.definition: The party or contract that checks a proof against a public statement and accepts or rejects it. Verification is cheap by design, which is what lets an onchain contract validate work done offchain.
verifier.morph_note: ZK contexts distinguish heavily between prover and verifier; must be non-interchangeable

zero-knowledge.definition: Describes a proof that convinces a verifier a statement is true while revealing nothing beyond that fact. On Ethereum the technique is used for privacy and, more often, for succinctly proving that offchain execution was correct.

zero-knowledge proof.definition: A zero-knowledge proof is a cryptographic method that allows an individual to prove that a statement is true without conveying any additional information.
zero-knowledge proof.translation_note: Cryptographic proof that something is true without revealing the underlying data.

aliases.note: Casual short form; expand on first use.

zero-knowledge proof.note: ZKP is the common acronym. ZK-proof (hyphenated, lowercase) is the accepted short form. Follow first-mention rule: spell out then use acronym.

zero-knowledge rollup.definition: A rollup of transactions that use validity proofs to offer increased layer 2 transaction throughput while using the security provided by Mainnet (layer 1). Although they can't handle complex transaction types, like optimistic rollups, they don't have latency issues because transactions are provably valid when submitted.

zk-snark.definition: A succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge: a proof that is small and fast to verify no matter how large the computation it attests to. Many constructions require a trusted setup to generate their parameters.

zk-stark.definition: A scalable transparent argument of knowledge. It needs no trusted setup and relies only on hash functions, which also makes it resistant to quantum attack, at the cost of larger proofs than a SNARK.

zkevm.definition: An implementation of the Ethereum Virtual Machine whose execution can be proved with a zero-knowledge proof. It lets a rollup run ordinary EVM bytecode and post a validity proof that Ethereum can verify cheaply.
zkevm.note: Zero-Knowledge Ethereum Virtual Machine. Technical identifier, keep Latin.

application binary interface (abi).definition: A JSON file that defines the functions and variables included in a smart contract. The ABI allows bytecode to be mapped into human-readable formats.

bytecode.definition: Code expressed in a compact, numeric form so that it can be executed efficiently by the EVM.

call data.definition: Data sent along with a transaction to a smart contract
call data.translation_note: 'Phone data' or 'shouting data' mistranslations in some languages
call data.note: "call data" in prose (two words). In code: `calldata` (lowercase) or `CALLDATA` (uppercase). These are distinct representations of the same concept.

composability.definition: The property that contracts can call one another freely, so applications can be assembled from existing pieces without permission. It is why DeFi protocols build on each other so readily, and also why a flaw in one can propagate to others.

composable.definition: Describes a contract or protocol designed so that others can build on top of it and combine it with further components. Standard interfaces such as ERC-20 are what make composability practical.

constructor.definition: The function run once when a contract is deployed, used to set initial state and immutable values. Its code is not part of the deployed bytecode and cannot be called again afterward.

contract.definition: Short for smart contract: code and state deployed at an address on Ethereum, which executes exactly as written whenever it is called. It is not a legal agreement.
contract.translation_note: Smart contract -- code deployed on the blockchain. NOT a legal agreement.

contract account.definition: An account containing code that executes whenever it receives a transaction from another account (EOA or contract).

contract creation transaction.definition: A special transaction that includes a contract's initiation code. The recipient is set to `null` and the contract is deployed to an address generated from the user address and `nonce`. that is used to register a contract and record it on the Ethereum blockchain.

deploy.definition: To publish a contract's bytecode to Ethereum, creating an account at a deterministic address that holds the code. Deployment is itself a transaction and costs gas.
deploy.translation_note: To publish a smart contract to the blockchain. Similar to software deployment.

deployment.definition: The act of publishing a contract to a network, and by extension the particular instance that results. The same source can be deployed many times, at different addresses and on different chains.

deposit contract.definition: The gateway to staking on Ethereum. The deposit contract is a smart contract on Ethereum that accepts deposits of ETH and manages validator balances. A validator cannot be activated without depositing ETH into this contract. The contract requires ETH and input data. This input data includes the validator public key and withdrawal public key, signed by the validator private key. This data is needed for a validator to be identified and approved by the proof-of-stake network.

ethereum virtual machine (evm).definition: A stack-based virtual machine that executes bytecode. In Ethereum, the execution model specifies how the system state is altered given a series of bytecode instructions and a small tuple of environmental data. This is specified through a formal model of a virtual state machine.
ethereum virtual machine (evm).translation_note: Stack-based runtime that executes smart contract bytecode. 'EVM' stays Latin, full name translates.

event.definition: A logging mechanism in Solidity. Emitting an event writes an entry to the transaction's logs, which offchain applications can index and subscribe to but contracts cannot read back.
event.translation_note: In Solidity: a logging mechanism in smart contracts. NOT a calendar event.

evm assembly language.definition: A human-readable form of EVM bytecode.
evm assembly language.note: EVM follows acronym casing within this term.

fallback function.definition: A default function called in the absence of data or a declared function name.

formal-verification.definition: Proving mathematically that code satisfies a specification for all inputs, rather than testing a sample of them. It is used on high-value contracts and on the protocol's own specifications.
formal-verification.note: Mathematical proof that smart contract code meets its specification. Academic term.

gas optimization.definition: The practice of writing efficient smart contract code to minimize gas costs
gas optimization.translation_note: 'Making gas better' is a common mistranslation; means reducing costs

immutable.definition: Unable to be changed once set. Deployed contract code is immutable, which is why upgradeability requires an explicit pattern such as a proxy, and why bugs cannot simply be patched in place.

immutable deployed code problem.definition: Once a contract's (or library's) code is deployed, it becomes immutable. Standard software development practices rely on being able to fix possible bugs and add new features, so this represents a challenge for smart contract development.

kevm.definition: A formal, executable specification of the EVM written in the K framework. It serves both as a precise definition of EVM semantics and as a basis for verifying contracts against it.

library.definition: A special type of contract that has no payable functions, no fallback function, and no data storage. Therefore, it cannot receive or hold ether, or store data. A library serves as previously deployed code that other contracts can call for read-only computation.
library.translation_note: In Solidity: reusable deployed code that other contracts can call. NOT a book library.

log.definition: An entry written to a transaction's receipt when a contract emits an event, made up of indexed topics and data. Logs are cheaper than storage and are meant for offchain consumers; contracts cannot read them.
log.translation_note: In Solidity: data emitted by events. NOT a physical log or diary.

opcode.definition: A single instruction in the Ethereum Virtual Machine, such as ADD or SSTORE, each with a defined gas cost. Compiled contract bytecode is a sequence of opcodes.
opcode.translation_note: Operation code -- a single instruction in the EVM. Keep Latin in code contexts.

overflow.definition: What happens when an arithmetic result exceeds the range of its type and wraps around. Solidity has reverted on overflow by default since version 0.8; earlier code needed libraries such as SafeMath.

precompile.definition: Specialized contract built into the EVM at a fixed address
precompile.translation_note: Must avoid confusion with 'pre-compiled code' in general software development

proxy contract.definition: A contract that holds the state and the address users interact with, while delegating its logic to a separate implementation contract. Because the implementation address can be changed, the pattern makes otherwise immutable code upgradeable, and it introduces an admin who can change that code.

reentrancy.definition: A vulnerability where a contract calls out to another contract that calls back in before the first has finished updating its state, letting the attacker act on stale values. The usual defenses are to update state before making external calls, or to use a reentrancy guard.

reentrancy guard.definition: A mechanism to prevent reentrancy attacks in smart contracts
reentrancy guard.translation_note: Often translated as 're-entry shield'; needs precise security term

require.definition: A Solidity statement that checks a condition and reverts the transaction, with an optional message, if it fails. It is the standard way to enforce preconditions such as access control or input validity.
require.translation_note: Solidity keyword that checks conditions in smart contracts. Keep as-is in code contexts.

revert.definition: To abort execution and undo every state change a transaction made, while still consuming the gas used up to that point. Contracts revert deliberately to reject invalid operations, optionally returning an error.

singleton.definition: A computer programming term that describes an object of which only a single instance can exist.

smart contract.definition: A smart contract is a program that automatically executes agreements on a blockchain, like a self-enforcing digital contract.
smart contract.translation_note: Self-executing code deployed on Ethereum. Combines 'smart' (automated) + 'contract' (agreement encoded as code).

solidity.definition: A procedural (imperative) programming language with syntax that is similar to JavaScript, C++, or Java. The most popular and most frequently used language for Ethereum smart contracts. Created by Dr. Gavin Wood.
solidity.translation_note: Programming language for Ethereum smart contracts. Proper noun, keep Latin.

solidity inline assembly.definition: EVM assembly language in a Solidity program. Solidity's support for inline assembly makes it easier to write certain operations.

source-code-verification.definition: Publishing a contract's source and compiler settings and showing that recompiling them reproduces the deployed bytecode. It is what lets a block explorer display readable source for an address, so users can check what the code actually does.
source-code-verification.note: Process of proving deployed bytecode matches published source code.

state.definition: A snapshot of all balances and data at a particular point in time on the blockchain, normally referring to the condition at a particular block.

state-trie.definition: The Merkle Patricia trie holding every account's nonce, balance, code hash, and storage root. Its root hash is committed to in each block header, so the entire state can be proved against a single value.
state-trie.note: Merkle Patricia trie storing all Ethereum account state.

storage-trie.definition: The per-contract Merkle Patricia trie holding that contract's storage slots. Its root is recorded in the account's entry in the state trie, so contract storage is committed to indirectly by the block header.
storage-trie.note: Per-account trie storing contract storage data.

upgradeable contract.definition: A contract designed so its logic can be replaced after deployment, usually through a proxy that delegates to a changeable implementation. It allows fixes and new features at the cost of introducing a party who can change the rules.

vyper.definition: A high-level programming language with Python-like syntax. Created by Vitalik Buterin.

airdrop.definition: A distribution of tokens to a set of addresses, usually chosen by past activity, without the recipients paying for them. Airdrops are used to bootstrap ownership and to reward early users.

allowance.definition: The amount of an ERC-20 token that one address has authorized another to spend on its behalf. A contract must be granted an allowance with approve before it can move a user's tokens.

approve.definition: The ERC-20 function that sets how much of your balance another address may spend. An unlimited approval is convenient but leaves those tokens exposed if the approved contract is later compromised.

burn.definition: To remove tokens from circulation permanently, either by sending them to an unspendable address or by a contract reducing total supply. Since EIP-1559, the base fee of every Ethereum transaction is burned.

claim.definition: The act of collecting tokens from an airdrop, reward, or vesting contract
claim.translation_note: Transitions from action (verb) to right (noun) to status (adjective); requires distinct forms
claim.morph_note: Action(v) to right(n) to status(adj); each needs specific phrasing in Asian languages

collectible.definition: A token, usually non-fungible, held for its uniqueness or provenance rather than as a financial instrument. Its metadata and image are typically stored offchain and referenced by the token URI.

dai.definition: A dollar-pegged stablecoin created by locking collateral in the Maker protocol's contracts rather than by a company holding reserves. Its peg is maintained through overcollateralization and liquidations.

fractionalization.definition: Dividing a single NFT or asset into multiple smaller, tradeable units

fungible token.definition: A token whose units are interchangeable, so any one unit is worth exactly as much as another. ERC-20 is the standard interface for fungible tokens on Ethereum.

governance token.definition: A token granting voting power over a protocol's decisions in proportion to the amount held or delegated. Holding one is a claim on influence, not necessarily on revenue or assets.

lp token.definition: A token issued to a liquidity provider representing their share of a pool. Redeeming it returns the underlying assets plus the provider's accrued share of fees.
lp token.note: LP = liquidity provider (acronym, always uppercase). Token is standard.

mint.definition: Minting is the process of creating new tokens and bringing them into circulation so that they can be used. It's a decentralized mechanism to create a new token without the involvement of the central authority.
mint.morph_note: Lacks direct financial equivalent in non-Western languages

minting.definition: Creating new tokens and assigning them to an address, increasing the total supply. Access to minting is a key permission: an unrestricted mint function lets whoever holds it dilute every other holder.
minting.morph_note: Lacks direct financial equivalent in non-Western languages

non-fungible token (nft).definition: A unique digital item you can own, like art or collectibles, verified by blockchain technology.
non-fungible token (nft).translation_note: Unique digital token proving ownership. 'NFT' stays Latin in most contexts.

poap.definition: Proof of Attendance Protocol is used to create a digital collectible (NFT) that proves you attended a specific event or activity.
poap.note: Proof of Attendance Protocol. Product/project name. Does not need to be spelled out -- "POAP" is widely recognized.

soulbound token (sbt).definition: A token that cannot be transferred once issued, so it stays with the account that received it. The design suits credentials, memberships, and reputation, where transferability would defeat the purpose.

token.definition: A tradable virtual good defined in smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain.
token.translation_note: A digital asset on Ethereum following a standard (ERC-20, ERC-721). NOT a physical coin or voucher.

token factory.definition: A token factory is a smart contract that facilitates the creation of tokens within a specific standard, such as ERC-20, ERC-721, or ERC-1155. The smart contract acts as a template, allowing users to deploy new tokens with custom parameters like name, symbol, supply, and extra functionality without creating a new smart contract from scratch.

token uri.definition: The URI recorded onchain that points to a token's metadata, usually a JSON document with a name, description, and image. Because that metadata generally lives offchain, its permanence depends on where the URI points.
token uri.note: URI = universal resource identifier (acronym, always uppercase in copy). Code usage may differ (tokenURI, token_uri).

tokenization.definition: Representing an asset or a right as a token on a blockchain so it can be transferred and used programmatically. When the underlying asset is offchain, the token is only as meaningful as the claim behind it.

transfer.definition: Moving tokens or ETH from one address to another. In ERC-20 it is also the name of the standard function, and of the event emitted when a balance changes.
transfer.translation_note: Moving tokens between addresses. In ERC-20 context, a specific function name.

usdc.definition: A dollar-pegged stablecoin issued by Circle and backed by reserves held offchain. Because the issuer controls the contract it can freeze balances, a trust assumption a decentralized stablecoin does not carry.

utility token.definition: A token whose purpose is use within a specific network or application, for example paying fees or accessing a service, rather than representing equity or a claim on assets.

vesting.definition: A schedule by which tokens are gradually released to their owners over time
vesting.translation_note: Often translated as 'clothing' (from Latin root) or 'investment'

wbtc.definition: Wrapped bitcoin: an ERC-20 token on Ethereum backed one for one by BTC held in custody. It lets bitcoin be used in Ethereum applications, at the cost of trusting the custodian and merchant network behind it.

wrapped token.definition: A blockchain-based token that represents another cryptocurrency or asset on a different network. For example, Wrapped Ether (WETH) represents ether (ETH) in a format that complies with Ethereum's ERC-20 token standard. The original asset is securely locked by a smart contract, and an equivalent wrapped token is minted. This mechanism enables interoperability within and between blockchains, allowing assets like ETH to be used seamlessly in decentralized applications while retaining their value.

base fee.definition: Every block has a reserve price known as the 'base fee'. It is the minimum gas fee a user must pay to include a transaction in the next block.

blob-fee.definition: The fee paid for the blob data in a blob-carrying transaction. It is priced in its own market that adjusts with blob demand, separately from the gas paid for execution, so the two do not compete directly.
blob-fee.note: Fee for blob data in EIP-4844 transactions. Separate from regular gas fees.

gas.definition: Gas is the fee paid for transactions and smart contracts on a blockchain, like Ethereum.
gas.translation_note: Unit measuring computational effort on Ethereum. Metaphor for fuel. NOT chemical/physical gas.

gas fee.definition: The amount paid to execute a transaction, equal to the gas used multiplied by the price per unit. Since EIP-1559 it splits into a base fee, which is burned, and a priority fee, which goes to the validator.

gas limit.definition: The maximum amount of gas a transaction or block may consume.

gas price.definition: Price in ether of one unit of gas specified in a transaction.

gwei.definition: Short for gigawei, a denomination of ether, commonly utilized to price gas. 1 gwei = 10<sup>9</sup> wei. 10<sup>9</sup> gwei = 1 ether.

intent.definition: A statement of the outcome a user wants, such as a desired trade result, rather than the exact transaction that produces it. Solvers compete to find the route that satisfies the intent, and the user signs only the outcome and its constraints.

internal transaction.definition: A transaction sent from a contract account to another contract account or an EOA (see message).

max fee.definition: The highest total price per unit of gas a sender is willing to pay, which caps what a transaction can cost. Anything above the base fee plus the priority fee is refunded.

max fee per gas.definition: The Max Fee is the absolute maximum amount a user is willing to pay per unit of gas (gwei) to get a transaction included in a block.

mempool.definition: The set of pending transactions a node has received but that are not yet in a block. Each node keeps its own view, and because the public mempool is visible, transactions sitting in it can be observed and front-run.
mempool.translation_note: Pool of pending transactions waiting to be included in a block.

nonce.definition: In cryptography, a value that can only be used once. An account nonce is a transaction counter in each account, which is used to prevent replay attacks.
nonce.translation_note: A counter ensuring each transaction is unique. Cryptographic term: 'number used once'.

pending transaction.definition: A transaction that has been broadcast and is waiting to be included in a block. It stays pending until a proposer includes it, until another transaction with the same nonce replaces it, or until it is dropped.

priority fee.definition: The tip per unit of gas paid directly to the block proposer on top of the base fee, to encourage inclusion. Raising it is how a sender competes for a place in a congested block.

receipt.definition: Data returned by an Ethereum client to represent the result of a particular transaction, including a hash of the transaction, its block number, the amount of gas used, and, in case of deployment of a smart contract, the address of the contract.
receipt.translation_note: A record of a transaction's execution result. Technical blockchain term.

solver.definition: A party that takes a user's intent and works out how to fulfill it, competing with other solvers to give the user the best outcome. Solvers absorb the complexity of routing and execution and are paid out of the surplus they generate.

tip.definition: Another name for the priority fee, the portion of a transaction fee that goes to the block proposer instead of being burned. It is not a gratuity in the everyday sense.
tip.translation_note: Priority fee paid to validators for faster inclusion. NOT a gratuity tip.

transaction.definition: Data committed to the Ethereum Blockchain signed by an originating account, targeting a specific address. The transaction contains metadata such as the gas limit for that transaction.
transaction.translation_note: A cryptographically signed data submission to the Ethereum blockchain. Not a financial transaction in the traditional sense.

transaction fee.definition:
A fee you need to pay whenever you use the Ethereum network. Examples include sending funds from your wallet or a dapp interaction, like swapping tokens or buying a collectable. You can think of this like a service charge. This fee will change based on how busy the network is. This is because validators, the people responsible for processing your transaction, are likely to prioritize transactions with higher fees – so congestion forces the price up.

At a technical level, your transaction fee relates to how much gas your transaction requires.

Reducing transaction fees is a subject of intense interest right now. See layer 2.

transaction hash.definition: The unique identifier of a transaction, computed as the hash of its signed contents. It is how a specific transaction is looked up in a wallet or a block explorer.

transaction pool.definition: The queue of pending transactions a node holds, more formally the mempool. Clients bound its size and order it by fee, dropping the least attractive transactions when it fills.

wei.definition: The smallest denomination of ether. 10<sup>18</sup> wei = 1 ether.
wei.note: Denomination of ether (lowercase). Named after Wei Dai (proper noun when referring to the person).

eth.definition: The native cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network. ETH is used to pay transaction fees (gas), to stake for validator participation, and as a unit of value.
eth.note: Ticker symbol for ether. Always Latin/uppercase across all languages per policy section 7.1.

trustlessness.definition: The property of a system that does not require participants to trust any central party or each other. In Ethereum, trustlessness comes from cryptographic guarantees and decentralized consensus rather than trust in a specific operator.

immutability.definition: The property of data or code that cannot be changed after it has been recorded. In Ethereum, deployed smart contracts and confirmed blocks are immutable absent a chain reorg.

self-destruct.definition: An EVM opcode (SELFDESTRUCT) that removes a smart contract from the active state. As of EIP-6780 (Dencun), self-destruct only fully removes a contract if called in the same transaction the contract was created in; otherwise it only transfers the balance.

cliff.definition: In a vesting schedule, an initial period during which no tokens are released. After the cliff ends, vesting begins (often immediately releasing the tokens that would have vested during the cliff).

slasher.definition: A validator or specialized node that detects and reports slashable offenses (double-voting, surround voting) by other validators. Submitting valid slashing evidence is rewarded with a portion of the offending validator stake.

sstore.definition: An EVM opcode that writes a 256-bit word to contract storage. Storage writes are the most expensive standard EVM operation (gas cost varies by whether the slot was previously zero or non-zero).

charles hoskinson.definition: One of the original co-founders of Ethereum, who left the project in 2014 over a disagreement about whether it should be run as a for-profit company, and who later founded Cardano. He appears in Ethereum content mostly in accounts of the project's early history.
charles hoskinson.translation_note: Major crypto founder with established transliterations in multiple languages.

gavin wood.definition: An Ethereum co-founder who wrote the Yellow Paper, the formal specification of the Ethereum Virtual Machine, and proposed Solidity, the main smart contract language. He later founded Polkadot and is credited with coining the term web3.
gavin wood.translation_note: Ethereum co-founder with widely established transliterations.

joseph lubin.definition: An Ethereum co-founder and the founder of ConsenSys, the company behind MetaMask and Infura. He appears in Ethereum content in accounts of the project's founding and of the tooling ecosystem built around it.
joseph lubin.translation_note: ConsenSys founder with established transliterations in multiple languages.

vitalik buterin.definition: The author of the 2013 Ethereum whitepaper and the project's best-known co-founder. He continues to publish research on Ethereum's scaling, consensus, and account abstraction roadmap, and that writing is cited directly throughout Ethereum documentation.
vitalik buterin.translation_note: Ethereum creator with universally established transliterations across non-Latin scripts.

wei dai.definition: A cryptographer and cypherpunk who described b-money in 1998, an early proposal for a distributed digital currency that the Bitcoin whitepaper cites as a precursor. The smallest denomination of ether, the wei, is named after him.
wei dai.translation_note: Famous cypherpunk with established Hanzi and transliterations.

aave.definition: A decentralized lending protocol built on Ethereum and several other networks. Depositors supply assets to shared liquidity pools and earn interest, while borrowers draw from those pools against collateral they have locked. It appears in Ethereum content as one of the most widely cited examples of DeFi lending.
aave.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

arbitrum.definition: A family of Ethereum layer 2 networks that use optimistic rollup technology to execute transactions cheaply and settle them on Ethereum. Contracts written for Ethereum run on it largely unchanged. It appears in Ethereum content as one of the most used layer 2 networks.
arbitrum.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

binance.definition: A large centralized cryptocurrency exchange, and the company behind the BNB Chain network. It appears in Ethereum content mainly as a place where people buy, sell, and custody ether and other tokens, in contrast to trading through a decentralized exchange.
binance.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

chrome.definition: A web browser developed by Google. It appears in Ethereum content because browser wallet extensions, MetaMask among them, are distributed for Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers, and installation instructions are usually written against it.
chrome.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

coinbase.definition: A centralized cryptocurrency exchange and custodian based in the United States. It appears in Ethereum content as one of the common places newcomers buy ether, and as the operator of Base, an Ethereum layer 2 network.
coinbase.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

consensys.definition: A software company founded by Joseph Lubin that builds Ethereum infrastructure and developer tooling. Its products include the MetaMask wallet and the Infura node service. It appears in Ethereum content wherever those tools are described.
consensys.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

cryptokitties.definition: One of the first widely used collectible applications on Ethereum, launched in 2017, in which players bought and bred unique digital cats. Its popularity congested the network and made transaction fees a mainstream topic. It appears in Ethereum content as the standard early example of an NFT application.
cryptokitties.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

dencun.definition: The upgrade activated in March 2024, combining Deneb on the consensus layer with Cancun on the execution layer. Its central change was EIP-4844, which introduced blobs and cut the cost of posting rollup data dramatically.
dencun.note: Ethereum upgrade combining Cancun (execution) and Deneb (consensus). Introduced blobs via EIP-4844.
dencun.translation_note: Major Ethereum networks and upgrades have established transliterations or calques in non-Latin communities.

discord.definition: A chat and voice platform organized into servers and channels. It appears in Ethereum content because most projects and developer communities run their support and coordination channels there.
discord.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

facebook.definition: A social network operated by Meta. It appears in Ethereum content largely as a point of comparison: a centralized platform that owns its users' accounts and data, set against the user-owned alternative that web3 describes.
facebook.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

filecoin.definition: A decentralized storage network whose participants are paid in its native token to store and serve files. It appears in Ethereum content as one of the options for holding data that is too large or too expensive to keep onchain, alongside IPFS and Arweave.
filecoin.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

goerli.definition: An Ethereum test network, now retired in favor of Sepolia and Holesky. It let developers deploy and test contracts using valueless test ether rather than spending real funds on Mainnet. It appears mainly in older documentation and tutorials.
goerli.translation_note: Major Ethereum networks and upgrades have established transliterations or calques in non-Latin communities.

holesky.definition: An Ethereum test network launched in 2023, sized to mirror Mainnet's validator set so that staking setups, infrastructure, and client upgrades can be rehearsed at realistic scale. Its test ether has no value. It took over the role Goerli had filled.
holesky.translation_note: Major Ethereum networks and upgrades have established transliterations or calques in non-Latin communities.

lido.definition: A liquid staking protocol. Users stake ether through it without running a validator themselves and receive a token representing the staked balance, which keeps earning rewards while remaining usable elsewhere in DeFi. It appears in Ethereum content as the largest example of liquid staking.
lido.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

makerdao.definition: The decentralized organization that created and governs DAI, a collateral-backed stablecoin on Ethereum. Holders of its governance token vote on the protocol's risk parameters. It appears in Ethereum content as an early and much-cited example of both a DAO and a decentralized stablecoin.
makerdao.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

microsoft.definition: A large software company. It appears in Ethereum content mostly through the tools developers use rather than through Ethereum itself: Windows as a platform for running clients, and Visual Studio Code and GitHub as where much Ethereum code is written and hosted.
microsoft.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

netflix.definition: A video streaming service. It appears in Ethereum content only as a familiar example of a conventional centralized web application, used to contrast with a dapp that runs on a decentralized network.
netflix.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

opensea.definition: A marketplace for buying and selling NFTs, mostly those issued on Ethereum and its layer 2 networks. It appears in Ethereum content as the best-known example of an NFT marketplace.
opensea.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

optimism.definition: An Ethereum layer 2 network built as an optimistic rollup, and the collective that governs it. It also maintains the OP Stack, the codebase other teams reuse to launch their own rollups. It appears in Ethereum content both as a specific network and as the origin of the optimistic rollup design.
optimism.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

paypal.definition: An online payments company. It appears in Ethereum content as a familiar reference point for what a centralized payment intermediary does, and as the issuer of a dollar stablecoin on Ethereum.
paypal.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

polygon.definition: A set of Ethereum scaling networks and the organization that builds them, best known for a proof-of-stake sidechain that was later joined by zero-knowledge rollup networks. It appears in Ethereum content as one of the common places to transact when Mainnet fees are high.
polygon.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

reddit.definition: A discussion site organized into topic-based communities. It appears in Ethereum content because several of the largest Ethereum discussion communities are hosted there.
reddit.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

ropsten.definition: An early Ethereum test network that mirrored Mainnet's proof-of-work consensus. It was retired in 2022, once Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake, and survives only in older documentation and tutorials.
ropsten.translation_note: Major Ethereum networks and upgrades have established transliterations or calques in non-Latin communities.

starknet.definition: An Ethereum layer 2 network built as a validity rollup, using STARK proofs to demonstrate to Ethereum that offchain execution was correct. Its contracts are written in Cairo rather than Solidity. It appears in Ethereum content as one of the main zero-knowledge rollup networks.
starknet.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

telegram.definition: A messaging app with large public channels and groups. It appears in Ethereum content because many projects run announcement channels and community groups there, and because impersonating those channels is a common scam.
telegram.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

twitter.definition: A microblogging platform, renamed X in 2023. It appears in Ethereum content because a great deal of protocol discussion, upgrade announcement, and project communication happens there, and because older material still refers to it by its former name.
twitter.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

youtube.definition: A video hosting platform operated by Google. It appears in Ethereum content as where conference talks, client walkthroughs, and tutorial material are published.
youtube.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

zksync.definition: An Ethereum layer 2 network built as a zero-knowledge rollup, and the ZK Stack codebase used to launch further networks that settle to Ethereum. It appears in Ethereum content as one of the main zero-knowledge rollup networks.
zksync.translation_note: Major consumer-tier brand or project with officially adopted or widely established native-script forms.

validate.note: CN/VI: technical 'validation' vs 'validator' role uses different semantic registers

bridge.note: Physical bridge noun vs functional/computing verb; HU/FI agglutinative suffixes change

mint.note: Lacks direct financial equivalent in non-Western languages

swap.note: DE/NL: noun (Tausch) and verb (tauschen) differ; DeFi context needs technical synonyms

fork.note: Often loanword as noun but translated as 'divergence' as verb in RU/PL

vote.note: Governance: 'ballot'(n) vs 'act of voting'(v) use different stems in Finno-Ugric

hash.note: Usually loanword noun; verb often 'calculate the checksum' in formal docs

sync.note: Long formal word for noun vs short English-derived slang for verb/action

attest.note: Ethereum 'attestation' is a specific object; general verb confuses with legal witnessing

propose.note: 'Block proposer' translates differently than general 'to propose an idea'

verify.note: ZK contexts distinguish heavily between prover and verifier; must be non-interchangeable

slash.note: Metaphorical penalty; action vs state require different idioms in TH/HI

build.note: 'Block builder' is specialized MEV role; 'constructing' vs 'software building' differ

withdraw.note: Action vs resulting transaction are grammatically distinct in Arabic

finalize.note: 'Finality' is chain property; 'finalized' is block state; must distinguish from 'finishing'

chain.note: Prefixes 'on-'/'off-' become complex prepositional phrases in TR/HU

claim.note: Action(v) to right(n) to status(adj); each needs specific phrasing in Asian languages
